description: Three-way merge scenarios for Claude Code JSONL transcripts. Inputs are windows of the recorded fixtures in this directory, optionally patched by the listed ops; expectations were produced by the reference implementation and checked against the merge postcondition and the four algebraic laws.

cases.note: Merging cli255Session.jsonl (272 lines of a real Desktop session) with itself returns the file untouched: the merge is the identity on an unchanged tree.
Merging cli255Isolated.jsonl (10 lines written by CLI 2.1.255) with itself returns the file untouched: the merge is the identity on an unchanged tree.
Merging cli232Isolated.jsonl (8 lines written by CLI 2.1.232) with itself returns the file untouched: the merge is the identity on an unchanged tree.
Merging cli255Subagent.jsonl (12 sidechain lines) with itself returns the file untouched: the merge is the identity on an unchanged tree.
Merging cli255Journal.jsonl (16 journal lines that carry neither uuid nor timestamp) with itself returns the file untouched: the merge is the identity on an unchanged tree.
Ours kept writing while theirs stayed at line 29 of cli255Session: every line ours added is new to base, so the result is ours byte for byte.
The mirror of oursSuperset: theirs holds lines 29..51 of cli255Session that ours never saw, and they are appended after the shared spine.
The roadmap gate. base is cli255Session[0,37), ours advanced to line 45, theirs advanced to line 51 without ever seeing lines 37..44; the merge must rebuild the original window [0,51) exactly.

reconstructTails with the tails swapped between the machines: the later tail is on ours, so theirs' lines 37..44 have to be spliced in ahead of it by timestamp and the original window [0,51) still comes out.

cli255Session lines 147 (queue-operation at 10:49:05.366) and 148 (system/stop_hook_summary stamped 10:13:52.463, half an hour earlier) land on different machines; head merge sorts by timestamp, so 148 is emitted before 146 and 147 and the recorded pair order is not preserved.

Both machines added turns from the same base cli255Session[0,46): theirs wrote lines 46..51 (10:07:11) and ours lines 56..59 (10:07:18), so theirs' block is spliced in before ours' and tail_side (ours) differs from visible (theirs, the side holding the leaf of the last last-prompt).

A fork whose newest last-prompt (cli255Session line 29) still points at a leaf both machines share, so visible is null even though tail_side is theirs: neither branch owns what the reader is looking at.

An interrupted write left ours 200 bytes short, so cli255Session line 44 stands as 541 unterminated bytes; the partial line is discarded, counted in ours.truncated, and the whole record comes back from theirs.
Both sides were cut mid line at once (ours inside line 44, theirs inside line 50); each side's torn record is simply missing and the merge still joins the two intact prefixes.
cli255Isolated with the final newline shaved off on all three sides: the last record becomes a tail and is dropped everywhere, so a file that never got its newline loses its last line.
Ours is a single line with no newline at all, so it contains zero records and 161 tail bytes; the merge takes everything from theirs instead of treating the fragment as data.
Ours is empty while base is a full cli255Isolated: without the absent side guard every base line would read as deleted by ours, so the guard drops base and the session survives whole.

Ours is two queue-operation lines from cli232Isolated -- a different machine's file with no uuid in common with base; it is treated as absent, base is dropped, and both files are kept side by side rather than one erasing the other.
The byte identical atis-latch line of cli255Isolated appears three times on ours and five times on theirs: copies are keyed by ordinal, so the result holds five, the maximum, and not eight.
Ours deleted cli255Session line 50 while theirs still has it; the line is nobody's parent, so the deletion is respected and counted as dropped on theirs.
The mirror of deletedByOursThreeWay: theirs deleted line 50, the deletion wins over ours' copy, and the counter lands on ours.

Ours deleted cli255Session line 49, whose uuid 7240275d is the parentUuid of the surviving line 50; the ancestor is resurrected from theirs, so the chain is never broken -- note it comes back after its own child, because head merge places it by timestamp.
The mirror of deletedAncestorResurrected: theirs is the side that deleted the ancestor, so the line comes back from ours and the resurrection is counted on the ours side.
The mirror of absentSideGuard: theirs is the empty side, so the guard marks theirs absent and the whole session survives from ours.
Line 6 of cli255Isolated was rewritten on theirs only; base arbitrates -- ours still equals base, so theirs' bytes win with no conflict.
Both machines rewrote line 6 of cli255Isolated differently; neither matches base, so both bytes are kept, ours first, and the uuid is reported as a conflict instead of one edit being lost.

The keep-both output of conflictSameUuid is merged again against the original base and against a machine that only has its own half: the pair survives unchanged and no new conflict is reported, so keep-both is a fixed point rather than a doubling loop.
One half of a settled keep-both pair is edited again on ours only; base arbitration applies per ordinal, so the edited half takes ours' bytes while the untouched half stays put.
Line 6 of cli255Isolated appears twice on ours with the same uuid; the ordinal keeps the two copies apart, so the duplicate is preserved rather than silently collapsed.
A constructed line carrying two top-level uuid fields fails to parse, so it is keyed by its bytes and counted as opaque instead of claiming either uuid.
A constructed line with a duplicated type field: type is one of the fields the merge reads, so the head cannot be trusted and the line is kept by its bytes (opaque) instead of claiming its uuid.
A constructed line with a duplicated cwd field: the merge never reads cwd, so the duplicate is ignored (last value wins, as in the reader) and the line keeps its uuid identity.
A top-level JSON array is never parsed -- the head gate only opens on '{' -- so it is keyed by bytes and counted as opaque even though it is valid JSON holding a uuid.
A timestamp of 1e400 puts the number out of range, which is a parse error; the line goes opaque and keeps its bytes as its key rather than being rounded to infinity.
Raw bytes ending in a lone 0xD0 -- a line cut in the middle of a two byte character and then newline-terminated by the next write -- are not UTF-8, so the line is opaque and survives byte for byte.
A line that is not JSON at all is still carried into the result: the merge never discards bytes it cannot read.

appendLines: not json at all -- a half written line from a crashed writer

cases.note: The same record written by a Windows writer carries a trailing CR; the CR is JSON whitespace so the line still parses and keeps its uuid key, but the bytes differ from theirs, and base arbitration hands the CRLF form through unchanged while theirs' own new turn is still appended after it.
A line prefixed with a UTF-8 BOM never reaches the parser -- its first byte is not '{' -- so it is keyed by bytes, counted as opaque, and still kept.
A bare empty line between two records is a record of its own, keyed by its (empty) bytes: it is opaque, it is preserved, and it does not shift the keys of its neighbours.

Ours holds a system/compact_boundary; theirs added a turn stamped before it and another after it. Head merge places the earlier one ahead of the boundary, which before_boundary counts as one -- that is the line a compact would have hidden from the reader.
cli255Journal has neither uuid nor timestamp, so every line is keyed by its bytes and every at is empty; ours holds lines 0..7 and theirs 0..3 plus 8..15, and the whole journal comes back in order.
The same two-way append on cli255Subagent, whose lines all carry isSidechain true: a sidechain transcript merges by the same rules with no special casing.

State lines from other writers -- summary in both key orders, ai-title, tag, mode, relocated -- are keyed by bytes, so the two key orders of the same summary are two records and none of them is deduplicated.

The state block is rewritten on its own schedule by each machine: base holds four byte-identical custom-title lines, ours five and theirs three. A missing copy is not a deletion, so the result holds the larger count and nothing is reported as dropped.
A line whose uuid is the empty string is not a record: it is keyed by its bytes like any state line, so the two sides match it by copy number instead of by identity.
The compaction boundary comes from theirs this time: the reader reads the file, not its history, so every added record before that boundary is counted -- including the one ours added.

A last-prompt names a leaf of theirs, but theirs also carries a compaction boundary stamped later, so head merge puts the boundary after the prompt. The reader clears the remembered leaf there, and the visible branch falls back to the tail of the file.
The last last-prompt names a leaf that no record in the result carries: the visible branch is unknown rather than guessed from the tail.

A Windows editor rewrote the state block with CRLF endings: a state line is keyed by its bytes, so the CR makes it a different line and the block is kept twice. Nothing is lost, but this is the price of touching the store with an editor -- doctor checks core.autocrlf=false and `* -text` for exactly this reason. Not verified on Windows.
All three inputs empty: the result is zero bytes and every counter is zero.
